Hi Dad,

Here is what happened in AI today. Each item links to the full story, with plain-language explanations of anything unfamiliar. The links go to a website built especially for you, with a new edition every day, so do check it out.

Question of the day: Can a computer find the rhymes in a poem? It sounds easy: look at the ends of the lines and see which ones sound alike. But poets rhyme “roses” with “apricots” in Russian, and Shakespeare rhymed words that no longer sound the same. The answer is at the end of this email.

  • Amazon: hackers’ AI programs found an unknown security hole and broke in by themselves; Microsoft describes the tool behind many such attacks. Amazon has published a rare look inside an attack run by AI. Hackers gave a set of AI programs a list of university computers and one instruction: get control. Most attempts failed after hours of trying, but on one computer the programs found a security hole nobody knew about and broke in within minutes, with no human guiding them. Microsoft, describing a similar tool now used by government-backed hackers and criminals alike, advises defenders to plant fake targets and fake “successes” to fool the machine. Both accounts come from the companies themselves. Read more and the background.
  • US regulator allows SpaceX to launch up to a million satellites as data centres in orbit. The American regulator that licenses satellites has allowed Elon Musk’s SpaceX to launch up to one million satellites meant to work as AI data centres in orbit: about fifty times as many satellites as circle the Earth today. The deadlines are loose (the full number by 2040), and astronomers’ and environmental groups’ objections were mostly set aside. A permission is not a working system: nobody has yet shown that data centres in space can be built or would pay for themselves. Read more and the background.
  • New York bans toys with built-in AI chatbots for five years. New York State has banned toys with a built-in AI chatbot (talking soft animals, dolls and robots) for five years, the second American state to do so after California. A study out the same week tested five such toys: they told children they loved them, promised to keep secrets, and most would explain where to find matches or pills. The ban starts in 90 days, so the toys stay on sale this Christmas; the governor asks parents not to buy them. Read more and the background.
  • Forty-two American states try to stop a bankrupt chatbot company from auctioning its users’ private conversations. Character.AI, a company whose AI characters were popular with teenagers, has gone bankrupt and plans to auction nearly everything it owns on 1 December, including the private conversations of more than 21 million American accounts, over two million of them children’s. Forty-two states have asked the court to stop the sale: the company had promised not to sell users’ data, and the buyer would be free to resell it. The court has not ruled yet. Read more and the background.

Also on the website today: Head of Anthropic: handing the running of society to AI “is a bad idea”, New test: even the best AI assistants fail about four in ten everyday chores, Music service Tidal will delete 27 million AI-made songs and ban new ones.

Answer to the question of the day. Yes, and quite well, but not in the obvious way. An article in the Russian magazine Sistemny Blok describes RhymeTagger, a program written by the Czech verse scholar Petr Plecháč. The naive method, comparing the last sounds of each line, misses the inexact rhymes that modern poets love and trips over old poems whose words were once pronounced differently. So the program is not given rules about what rhymes. Instead it learns from the poems themselves. First it collects the last word of every line in a large collection of poetry and looks for pairs of words that keep turning up close together, far more often than chance would explain; those are very probably rhymes. From these pairs it works out which sounds tend to go together at the ends of words, and so learns, for instance, that an “s” and a “z” in the same position are often close enough for a poet. Then it goes through the poems again with this knowledge, finds more rhymes, learns from those, and repeats until nothing new turns up. Where old pronunciation gets in the way, it falls back on spelling and compares the last three letters. By its author’s tests it found more than 95% of rhymes in Czech poetry and more than 85% in English and French, and was wrong in fewer than 7% of cases. The magazine tried it on a poem by Mayakovsky: it caught an inexact rhyme correctly but was confused where the poet broke one line into three short steps. The lesson holds for much of today’s AI: nobody told the program what a rhyme is; it worked it out from many examples, and it stumbles on whatever looks unlike those examples. Sistemny Blok, “A program for finding rhymes: how it works and when it breaks” (article in Russian).
